text: An MCP server advertises its tools through tools/list. Each tool carries a name, a description and an inputSchema. The description is the only evidence the model has when deciding whether the tool is relevant, so a vague one means the tool is never called.

Zod constraints on a tool's input schema are enforced before the handler runs. A call with sides set to zero is rejected by the protocol layer and the model receives a correction it can act on, rather than an exception from inside your code.

MCP exposes three primitives and they differ by who initiates. A tool is chosen by the model mid-conversation. A resource is attached by the application on the user's behalf. A prompt is invoked explicitly by the user.

A server may annotate a tool with destructiveHint. That flag arrives over the network from a machine you do not control, so a host that reads it has given the key to whoever stands outside the door. Classification belongs to the host.

An allowlist that keys only on the tool name forces a choice between blocking every read and permitting every write. The verb usually lives in the arguments, so the gate has to open them and match on the payload.

Default-deny prompts on every unclassified call, and within about ninety seconds the operator is approving without reading. A gate that trains reflexive approval is worse than none, because it also supplies the feeling of safety.

Stopping an agent mid-run is a state problem rather than a control-flow one. The message array already contains the assistant turn with its tool_use blocks, so persisting it is the pause. Append the results later and the conversation is valid again.

If any call in a batch requires human sign-off, none of the batch executes. Running the safe ones first is faster, but a denial then leaves half the work done, which is far harder to explain to the person who pressed the button.

A refusal returned as the bare word denied causes the model to retry the identical call. Wording that says the operator declined it, do not attempt again, and explain the alternative turns a dead end into an answer.
Marking a failed tool result with is_error true makes the model treat it as a path to route around rather than a result to report as though it had succeeded.

Sub-agent delegation is one tool whose implementation is the agent loop calling itself. The child gets an empty conversation, the same toolbox and a single instruction, and returns one paragraph that the parent cannot distinguish from any other tool result.

A single loop processing 240 items failed to find any of 36 targets while spending 439,000 tokens. Three workers found all 36 for 248,000. The loop does not fail because there is more work; it fails because it re-sends everything it has already read on every iteration.

Context in a tool-use loop is a tape replayed each turn rather than a bucket filled once. A job reading n items over k iterations pays closer to n times k, so the iteration cap arrives long before the work is finished.
Recursion multiplies per-loop limits instead of adding them. An orchestrator allowed ten iterations that spawns three workers allowed ten each has quietly authorised forty model calls.

There is no depth counter. The child is started without the spawning tool in its list at all, so it cannot recurse for the same reason you cannot dial a number that was never printed. Prefer a design where the bad thing is unreachable over a check that catches it.

Three ceilings constrain three different resources: how many workers run at once, how many run in total, and what the whole tree is permitted to spend. Any one alone leaks, because concurrency without a total means sixty workers three at a time.

When a worker two levels down hits the gate, nobody is talking to it. Every approval belongs to the operator at the top, the child's reasoning travels up with it, and finished siblings are kept rather than re-run.
Sampling inverts the usual direction: the server asks your host to run a model call. It holds no key and no model. It has yours, which is why the ceiling has to live on the host side.

Because the ceiling reasons about an estimate before anything is sent, a refusal spends nothing at all. Across thirteen requested calls, eight were allowed at thirteen cents and five were refused at zero.

Destruction is a property of the verb, so gating on which tool was called works. Price is not. The same summarise call is a twentieth of a cent on a small corpus and forty cents on a large one, so the rule has to be a number.

This gate cannot pause. Somebody else's server is blocked inside a call and will time out within a minute, so freezing it deadlocks rather than suspends. The refusal is synchronous; the approval lands on the retry.

Opaque state handed to a client and echoed back is attacker-controlled input. Data does not stay yours by having been yours. Sign it, verify it, and on the host side pass the blob through without ever parsing it.

One wallet, many spenders, every draw labelled. Billing a server's model call to a separate per-server pot implies an ownership that does not exist, and lets a server sit in budget while the run as a whole is broke.

A fixed cosine cutoff discards material the corpus plainly contains. Cosine similarity is a relative measure whose scale shifts with question length and vocabulary overlap, so any constant is too strict for some queries and too loose for others.
Too strict fails silently. The answer never arrives and nothing records a reason, whereas too loose fails visibly through irrelevant citations you notice immediately.

Taking the best n results is scale-invariant. It does not matter whether today's strongest match scored 0.61 or 0.88, only which items are strongest relative to one another, which is the sole question the embedding can answer.

Instructing the model to answer only from supplied context, to say it does not know when the answer is absent, and to cite sources by filename is what makes returning the top n safe rather than an invitation to invent.

Verify abstention with deliberately out-of-scope questions phrased confidently. If any receives a confident answer, the constraint has stopped working, usually because someone raised n until the context became noise.

Chunking with overlap keeps a sentence that straddles a boundary retrievable from either side. Roughly 800 characters with 150 of overlap is a starting point, not a law, and the right size depends on how self-contained your paragraphs are.
Row level security belongs in the schema rather than in a convention that every query filters by owner. A predicate the database enforces survives a route somebody wrote at eleven at night.

A policy needs both a using clause and a with check clause. The first governs what can be read and modified; the second validates rows being written. Read isolation without write isolation is half a boundary.

A Postgres function declared security definer runs as its owner and bypasses row policies entirely. In a retrieval system that function builds the context for every answer, so one keyword silently disables the whole model.

Prove tenant isolation from a second account rather than by rereading the policies. Ask a question whose answer exists only in the first account's documents; the correct outcome is an explicit refusal with no sources cited.

Every iteration re-sends the whole conversation, so cost grows faster than the interesting part of the prompt. One breakpoint on the stable prefix cut the full-price equivalent from 7,540 tokens to about 4,004, a saving of 47 percent.

A cached prefix must be byte-identical to hit. Interpolating a timestamp or session identifier turns every hit into a miss with no error at all, only a larger bill, so build the tool list once outside the loop.

After caching, the reported input token count covers only the uncached remainder. The real prompt size is that figure plus the tokens written to cache plus the tokens read from it, weighted differently for price.

Below the minimum cacheable prefix the API silently declines to cache and reports zero tokens created. A short system prompt on its own never clears the floor, which is why the marker belongs after the tool definitions.

Define the seam by what the caller uses rather than what the dependency offers. An interface shaped like the vendor SDK is a second SDK you now maintain; one shaped like your own call site is four lines and cannot drift.
A pass-through implementation that simply invokes the function is enough to substitute for the durable execution engine in a test, because it preserves the only semantics the loop depends on.

A model client that always requests another tool call is the adversary the iteration ceiling exists to defend against. You cannot reliably produce that from a live model, let alone on demand in continuous integration for nothing.
Wrapping every unit of background work in its own checkpoint means a transient failure costs one step rather than the whole run. The unit of failure is a design decision, not a fact about the world.

Enabling retries makes idempotency a requirement. A step that inserts a row and then does something that can fail will insert that row twice, and the duplicate only appears the first time a retry happens in production.

A run that fails to enqueue leaves a queued row nothing will ever pick up, indistinguishable in the interface from one about to start. Still working and died four minutes ago must never look the same.
Writing each step as it happens and subscribing to the table gives the live view and the audit trail from one representation. Streaming from memory and persisting afterwards produces two that drift.

Every field in the extraction schema is nullable except the list. If the type system cannot express absence, uncertainty is not removed, only converted into a confident wrong answer, and a fabricated zero reconciles against nothing.
Print the shape as a literal rather than describing it in prose, and fence the untrusted document so its own text cannot read as further instruction.
Models are heavily trained to wrap output in code fences, so instructions reduce that without eliminating it. Six lines that strip the fence turn an intermittent unreproducible failure into nothing.

Returning an empty default when parsing fails produces a pipeline that appears to work and yields nothing useful. An exception carrying a sentence about what went wrong is worth more than a fallback that hides it.

BizTalk validated inbound messages against a schema before any orchestration logic saw them, because a bad message halfway through a multi-step process leaves partial state in three systems and no clean way to unwind.
The suspended message queue was a first-class place for failures to sit with enough context attached to diagnose them. Agent systems mostly rebuild this without noticing, and call it a trace.

Non-determinism at the routing layer is the genuine difference. The same input may take a different path and be right to, so replay-and-compare is not a correctness check and assertions belong on outcomes and cost.

If a release is one indivisible operation across four hundred stores, a single bad install makes the entire rollout suspect. Per-store units with their own verification and rollback turn an incident into a phone call.

The installer reporting success and the till actually working are different claims, and only one of them mattered. The same distinction separates an agent that returned a confident answer from one that was right.
A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately, which is what makes searching a corpus affordable and is also its ceiling: the document vector was computed without knowing what would be asked.
A cross-encoder runs attention across the query and the document together. Far more accurate and far too slow for a whole corpus, which is why the two compose as retrieve wide then rerank narrow.
BM25 saturates term frequency, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds much less than the second. Length normalisation stops long passages winning by accident, which is the classic chunking bug.
Fusing rankings by position rather than by score avoids normalising three distributions whose shape changes per query. Throwing the scores away is the point.
Recall answers whether the material was found at all, and a document the retriever never returned cannot be read by the model no matter how good the prompt is.
Only the ranking-sensitive measure distinguishes a reranker from the retriever beneath it, because the others are satisfied as soon as the right item appears anywhere in the window.
Averaging each query once rather than each judgement means one heavily annotated question cannot outvote seven lightly annotated ones.
